content: All studies were assessed to have an unclear risk of bias concerning the composite reference standard due to its imperfect accuracy and the varying definitions used by the primary study authors. Regarding applicability in the patient selection domain, 50% of studies were judged to have a high or unclear risk of bias because participants were exclusively evaluated as inpatients at tertiary care centers or because the clinical setting was unclear. For the applicability of the index test, most studies (72%) were judged to have low concern due to the standardized application of the index tests. However, 11 studies evaluating stool as a specimen for Xpert MTB/RIF or Xpert Ultra were judged to have an unclear risk of bias due to the absence of a standardized protocol for stool preparation. The applicability of the reference standard was considered a low concern for most studies (93%). Six studies, including 223 participants, were included to generate evidence about the detection of rifampicin resistance. All six studies evaluated only Xpert MTB/RIF and were conducted in high TB and high multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB) burden countries. Among these studies, 50% had a low risk of bias regarding patient selection, while all studies had a low risk of bias concerning the reference standard. The risk of bias for the reference standard was considered low if an automated process was used or if it was clear that the reference standard results were interpreted without knowledge of the index tests. However, all six studies raised applicability concerns regarding patient selection because participants were exclusively enrolled from inpatient or tertiary care centers. For the meta-analysis, 23 studies (6,612 participants) evaluated sputum specimens, 14 studies (3,468 participants) evaluated gastric specimens, four studies (1,125 participants) evaluated nasopharyngeal specimens, and 11 studies (1,592 participants) evaluated stool specimens. All these studies assessed Xpert MTB/RIF alone. Three studies (753 participants) evaluated both Xpert MTB/RIF and Xpert Ultra on frozen sputum specimens, and one study (195 participants) evaluated both tests on nasopharyngeal specimens. No studies evaluated Xpert Ultra alone for pulmonary TB or rifampicin resistance in children compared to microbiological reference standards (MRS) and composite reference standards (CRS). For extrapulmonary TB, 65 studies were included. A total of 63 studies (13,144 participants) evaluated Xpert MTB/RIF, including five that evaluated both Xpert MTB/RIF and Xpert Ultra. These studies assessed Xpert MTB/RIF in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), lymph node aspirates, lymph node biopsies, pleural fluid, urine, synovial fluid, peritoneal fluid, pericardial fluid, and blood. Of these studies, 39 (60%) were conducted in high TB burden countries, and 41 (63%) were conducted in high TB/HIV burden countries. The risk of bias was judged to be low in the domains of patient selection, index test, and flow and timing, but high or unclear in the reference standard domain due to the decontamination of sterile specimens before culture inoculation. Applicability concerns were high or unclear for most studies due to exclusive evaluation of participants as inpatients at tertiary care centers or unclear clinical settings. For lymph node TB diagnosis in children, six studies (210 participants) evaluated Xpert MTB/RIF against an MRS of smear or culture on lymph node specimens, and two studies (105 participants) evaluated it against a CRS. For TB meningitis, six studies (241 participants) evaluated Xpert MTB/RIF against culture on CSF, and two studies (155 participants) assessed it against a CRS that included clinical diagnosis. The certainty of evidence was judged to be very low for sensitivity and low for specificity for detecting both TB meningitis and lymph node TB. No studies evaluated the accuracy of Xpert Ultra for detecting lymph node TB or TB meningitis. For pulmonary TB in children, five studies (2,119 participants) evaluated the diagnostic accuracy of multiple Xpert MTB/RIF tests compared to a single test. Serious concerns were raised about indirectness due to patient enrollment from inpatient tertiary care settings, which may have included children with more advanced disease. Additionally, serious concerns were raised about imprecision due to the low number of children with pulmonary TB contributing to the analysis. Overall, the certainty of evidence was judged to be very low for sensitivity and moderate for specificity. For adults with pulmonary TB, six surveys evaluated Xpert MTB/RIF or Xpert Ultra against culture as the reference standard. These surveys included adults with chest X-ray abnormalities or symptoms suggestive of pulmonary TB. The certainty of evidence was judged to be low for sensitivity and moderate for specificity due to concerns about indirectness and imprecision. For cost-effectiveness, a systematic review identified 28 studies addressing the economic evaluation of molecular-based tests for TB diagnosis, including Xpert MTB/RIF and Xpert Ultra. Most studies assessed Xpert MTB/RIF in outpatient settings in African countries, with some studies conducted in Brazil, China, Germany, Hong Kong, India, South Africa, and the USA. The studies varied in their costing, effectiveness, and epidemiological parameters, making direct comparisons challenging. No studies assessed the cost-effectiveness of Xpert Ultra.
